common_name: Cathedral Mealycup Sage (Compact Early-Flowering Seed Salvia)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Cathedral is a compact, uniform bedding series that flowers earlier from seed than taller mealycup sage selections.

directions: Cathedral is a compact, early-flowering seed strain of mealycup sage bred for uniform bedding display, producing dense spikes of violet-blue, blue, or white flowers with the same soft, powdery-textured calyxes typical of the species, on a shorter, more front-of-border plant than taller selections like Evolution or Victoria. Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun after hardening off. It flowers continuously from early summer through fall with minimal deadheading, tolerating heat and drought well once established, and draws bees and butterflies throughout its long bloom season. Treat as a perennial in zones 8-10, where it often persists and reblooms for a second year, or as a heat-loving annual in cooler climates.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Vista Red Salvia (Early-Flowering Compact Bedding Salvia)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after all danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vista is a branching, well-filled series that flowers earlier and holds up better in heat than older tall salvia splendens strains.

directions: Vista Red is a compact, heavily branching selection of the classic bedding salvia, covering itself in dense spikes of vivid scarlet-red flowers from early summer through frost on a plant well-filled from the base rather than the leggy, single-stemmed habit of older tall Salvia splendens strains. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since it needs a long season to reach flowering size, and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade once frost danger has passed. It tolerates heat well for a bedding salvia and continues flowering through summer with regular watering and occasional deadheading of spent spikes. In zone 9 it is grown as a warm-season annual, though it may persist as a short-lived perennial in the mildest microclimates.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Extension — Annual Trial Gardens

planting.note: Plant container plants after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; AngelMist is a vegetatively propagated series bred for a larger, more vigorous, well-branched plant than seed-grown angelonia series like Serena.

directions: AngelMist is a vegetatively propagated angelonia series bred for a larger, more vigorous, and more heavily branched plant than seed-grown series, producing tall spikes of small, orchid-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, white, and bicolors over glossy, narrow foliage from early summer through the hottest, most humid stretch of the season without fading. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, and expect it to keep blooming with almost no deadheading needed, since spent flowers are inconspicuous along the spike. It is markedly heat- and humidity-tolerant, making it one of the most reliable summer bedding plants for the Gulf South, and tolerates drought well once established. In zone 9 it is typically grown as a warm-season annual, though it may survive a mild winter in sheltered spots.

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; SuperCal is an intergeneric cross between Calibrachoa and Petunia bred to combine the weather resistance of calibrachoa with the larger flower size of petunia.

directions: SuperCal is an intergeneric hybrid between calibrachoa and petunia, combining the small parent's rain- and heat-resistant flower coverage with larger, more petunia-like blooms and a more vigorous, mounding-to-trailing habit well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and mixed containers. It flowers continuously from spring through frost with little to no deadheading needed, since spent flowers dry up and drop cleanly rather than turning to mush the way many petunia flowers do in humid weather. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and feed regularly through the growing season, since heavy, continuous bloom draws down nutrients quickly in a container. It tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity better than most petunias, making it a strong choice for a summer-long hanging basket display.
sources: Pennsylvania State University Extension — Annual Trial Gardens
